title: Neighbors in al-Andalus
hook: Muslims, Jews and Christians shared cities and learning, alongside real tension and times of persecution

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Arabi, the mystic from Murcia who answered the philosopher yes, and then no. Your line was: the greatest master, some say. Did you let a question keep two answers? Day nine hundred forty-two.

A general sits in an army camp and writes a poem. In Hebrew. His name is Samuel ibn Naghrela. He is a Jew, he serves a Muslim king of Granada as vizier, the chief minister, and he leads that king's troops in the field. His Hebrew poems move in the meters of Arabic verse, and some were written on campaign: the night before a battle, the fear, the thanks for coming home alive. A Jewish commander, a Muslim court, Hebrew words in Arabic rhythms. That is one face of al-Andalus. Keep his family's name in mind, because his son's story shows the other face, and today needs both.
screen: `A JEWISH VIZIER WRITES A POEM.` → `HEBREW IN ARABIC METERS.` → `HIS SON'S STORY IS THE OTHER FACE.`

segments.voice: Start with the frame. The Qur'an calls Jews and Christians People of the Book, and under Muslim rule in al-Andalus they lived as protected communities. They kept their own worship, their own clergy, their own courts. They also paid a special tax and lived under limits a Muslim neighbor didn't. Protection and inequality, in the same arrangement. Now the sharing. At the court of Abd al-Rahman the Third, a Jewish physician named Hasdai ibn Shaprut served as a trusted diplomat. Jewish poets, Samuel among them, wrote Hebrew verse in the patterns of Arabic poetry. Philosophers of all three communities argued over the same Greek books, read in Arabic. And now the other side, said just as plainly. In Cordoba, some Christians who publicly denounced Islam were executed, and their community remembered them as martyrs. In Granada, a mob turned on the Jews of the city, and among the dead was the vizier Joseph, Samuel's own son. Later, under the Almohad rulers, Jews and Christians faced pressure to convert, and some fled; the family of the Jewish scholar Maimonides was among those who left. Christian kingdoms to the north, meanwhile, were pushing south by war. So which was it, harmony or persecution? The honest answer is both, at different times, in different cities, under different rulers. The Qur'an gives a reason for difference, in Pickthall's words: "We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Knowing one another includes knowing the hard chapters. Shared, and not simple.
screen: `PROTECTED, AND NOT EQUAL.` · `A JEWISH DIPLOMAT, ARABIC METERS.` · `MARTYRS, A MOB, A FAMILY THAT FLED.` · `THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.` · then, large: `SHARED, AND NOT SIMPLE.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to learn about your neighbors' history. Settle, and breathe. Think of a neighbor, a coworker, a classmate, someone whose family comes from a story different from yours. What do you actually know about where they come from? Let one honest question form: how did their people come to be here, what did they carry, what did they lose? Hold that question gently. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer. If you don't, just hold them in mind with good will. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Naghrela, the Jewish vizier and general who served a Muslim king of Granada and wrote Hebrew poems in Arabic meters, even on campaign. Today's word.
Your line: shared, and not simple. Today, look up one thing about the history of a community near you that isn't your own, and read past the first easy summary. Day nine hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims, Jews and Christians today remember al-Andalus in different ways; historians describe both its shared learning and its inequality and episodes of violence.

myth: al-Andalus was a perfect paradise of harmony
Jews and Christians were protected but not equal, and there were executions, a mob in Granada and forced conversions.
there was real sharing too: a Jewish diplomat at court, Hebrew poems in Arabic patterns, scholars reading the same books.
a Jewish vizier of Granada also led its troops and wrote Hebrew poems
Samuel ibn Naghrela served a Muslim king as vizier and commander, and wrote Hebrew verse in Arabic meters.

fork.setup: you're Samuel ibn Naghrela, a Jew serving a Muslim king of Granada, back from a campaign. you want to write about it. how do you write?
options: in Latin, like the churchmen to the north.
in Hebrew, in the meters of Arabic poetry.
not at all; a vizier doesn't write poems.
fork.reveal: Hebrew, shaped by Arabic meters. his poems show how close the neighbors' cultures had come; his son Joseph's death at the hands of a Granada mob shows how fragile it was.

original.note: Arabic: People of the Book, the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians.

trapdoor: what you thought: either a golden age of tolerance or a story of oppression.
what it means: neighbors sharing cities, words and books, under an arrangement of protection and inequality, with real violence at times.
what a scholar hears: dhimmi status, Hasdai ibn Shaprut, Samuel ibn Naghrela and his son Joseph, the Cordoba martyrs and the Almohads, held together.
